title: Social Security Disability Lawyer Cost: The $9,200 Fee Cap (2026)
description: How SSDI lawyers are paid: 25% of back pay capped at $9,200, fee agreements vs fee petitions, and the $123 user fee SSA deducts from the representative.
h1: How much does a Social Security disability lawyer cost?
summary: Under an SSA-approved fee agreement, a disability representative's fee is the lesser of 25% of your past-due benefits or $9,200, for favorable decisions issued on or after November 30, 2024. If there is no approved agreement, the representative files a fee petition and SSA sets a reasonable fee for the itemized work. SSA deducts a user fee of 6.3% capped at $123 (for payments on or after December 1, 2025) from the representative's payment, not from yours.
body:
How SSDI lawyers are paid

Social Security disability lawyers and non-attorney representatives are paid differently from almost any other lawyer: the Social Security Administration (SSA) must approve the fee, the fee normally comes out of your back pay, and there is a legal maximum. If you do not win benefits, there are usually no past-due benefits to take a fee from. A representative cannot simply bill you an hourly rate for work before the agency; the fee has to go through one of two SSA processes: a fee agreement or a fee petition [2].

The fee agreement: 25% capped at $9,200

Most representatives use a written fee agreement. SSA approves the fee if it does not exceed the lesser of 25% of your past-due benefits or $9,200, for favorable decisions issued on or after November 30, 2024 [1]. Earlier caps were $7,200 for decisions from November 30, 2022 to November 29, 2024, and $6,000 before that [4]. In May 2025 SSA kept the $9,200 cap and said it will publish a new notice only when it raises the cap; as of October 2026 we found no increase [3].

For SSA to approve the agreement, it must be filed before the first favorable decision, signed by you and the representative, and the decision must be fully or partially favorable with past-due benefits [1].

Example 1: past-due benefits of $24,000. 25% × $24,000 = $6,000, which is below $9,200, so the maximum fee is $6,000.

Example 2: past-due benefits of $48,000. 25% × $48,000 = $12,000, which is above $9,200, so the maximum fee is $9,200.

Back pay is the benefit that accrued before the decision. The fee is not taken from your future monthly checks.

The fee petition: when the agreement does not apply

If there is no fee agreement, SSA does not approve it, or its disapproval is upheld on review, the representative must file a fee petition to charge a fee [1]. The two processes are not interchangeable [2]. In a fee petition, the representative itemizes the services performed after the case ends and SSA sets a reasonable fee for them [5]. Fee petitions are more common when a case was long, went through several appeals, or ended with a small or no past-due award.

If your case goes on to federal court, the court can award a separate fee for the court work under 42 U.S.C. § 406(b) [5].

Fee agreement vs fee petition

The two SSA fee processes
Fee agreementFee petition
When it is filedBefore the first favorable decision [1]After the representative's work ends [5]
MaximumLesser of 25% of past-due benefits or $9,200 [1]A reasonable fee set by SSA for the services itemized [5]
Typical useMost initial claims and hearingsComplex or lengthy cases, or when the agreement is not approved

The user fee is paid by the representative, not you

When SSA pays an eligible representative directly out of your back pay, it deducts a user fee from the representative's payment. For direct payments made on or after December 1, 2025, the user fee is the lesser of 6.3% of the fee or $123, and the representative cannot pass it on to you [2]. The statute caps the percentage at 6.3% and adjusts the dollar limit with cost-of-living changes [5].

Example: a $6,000 authorized fee. 6.3% × $6,000 = $378, which is above $123, so SSA deducts $123 and pays the representative $6,000 − $123 = $5,877. Your cost is still $6,000.

Other costs to ask about

  • Out-of-pocket expenses. Medical records, consultative reports and copying can cost money. Ask whether the representative will charge you for them separately and when.
  • Appeals. Ask whether the fee agreement covers the hearing and the Appeals Council, and what happens if the case goes to federal court.
  • Disputes. If you think a fee is wrong, you can ask SSA to review the fee authorization. Representatives who want a higher fee must request review within 15 days of the fee notice [1].

Questions to ask before signing

  • Will you use a fee agreement, and is the fee the full 25% up to the cap or less?
  • Which expenses will I pay myself, and are they capped?
  • Do you handle the hearing yourself, and do you take cases to federal court?

Do you need a representative?

You can apply on your own, and many people do at the first stage. Representation is more common at the hearing stage, where medical evidence and vocational questions decide the case. Because the fee is capped and contingent on back pay, cost is rarely the reason not to get help, but the cap does mean that a representative's fee can take a large share of a small back-pay award. For low-income help, see the legal aid guide; for workplace injuries, see workers' comp lawyer cost.

faq.q: Do I pay an SSDI lawyer if I lose?
faq.a: Under a fee agreement the fee is a share of past-due benefits, so if you are not awarded back pay there is normally no fee from it. You may still owe out-of-pocket expenses such as medical record charges if your agreement says so.

faq.q: Can an SSDI lawyer take more than $9,200?
faq.a: Not under a fee agreement for decisions on or after November 30, 2024. A higher amount is possible only through a fee petition approved by SSA, or for separate federal court work approved by the court.

faq.q: Is the fee taken from my monthly checks?
faq.a: No. The fee comes from past-due benefits, the back pay that built up before your approval, not from ongoing monthly payments.

faq.q: What is the SSA user fee?
faq.a: A charge SSA deducts when it pays a representative directly: the lesser of 6.3% of the fee or $123 for payments on or after December 1, 2025. The representative may not pass it on to you.
